authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro candidate authoring; human review required

items.prompt: A graph has 200,000 vertices and 260,000 undirected edges. The main operation is repeatedly iterating over the neighbors of a reached vertex. Which representation best matches that operation profile?

options.text: One flat list of edge pairs, scanned from the beginning whenever a vertex is expanded.
A 200,000 × 200,000 adjacency matrix.
An adjacency list with one neighbor collection per vertex.
One parent pointer per vertex, because every traversal can be treated as a tree.

feedback.reason: Sparse neighbor iteration is the decisive operation, so adjacency lists expose exactly the incident edges without quadratic storage.

blocks.text: Store the neighbors that actually exist

items: An adjacency list keeps one collection per vertex and stores each undirected edge in both endpoint collections.
With V = 200,000 and E = 260,000, it needs O(V + E) structural space: vertex entries plus about 2E neighbor entries.
Expanding vertex v inspects only degree(v) neighbors; over a full traversal, all adjacency-list scans total O(V + E).

blocks.text: A 200,000 × 200,000 matrix reserves 40 billion cells, and finding one vertex's neighbors requires scanning its 200,000-cell row. A flat edge list is compact input storage, but expanding one vertex would rescan unrelated edges unless the list were first indexed—which would effectively build an adjacency structure.

blocks.title: Representation rule
blocks.text: For a sparse graph dominated by neighbor iteration, use storage proportional to actual vertices and edges.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.adjacency_matrix: A matrix gives constant-time edge membership, but its quadratic storage and row scans are disproportionate for this sparse graph.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.edge_list: An edge list is compact, but repeated neighbor expansion would rescan unrelated edges and obscure the traversal cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.parent_array: A general graph may contain cycles and multiple incoming edges; a parent array does not represent all legal neighbors.

items.prompt: A directed graph has 2,000 vertices, is close to complete, and a later phase performs millions of queries of the form ‘does edge u → v exist?’. Memory for roughly four million booleans is explicitly available. Which representation is justified?

options.text: An unsorted adjacency list, because matrices are categorically wrong for graphs.
An adjacency matrix indexed by [u][v].
Run BFS from every vertex; BFS is faster than DFS, so the representation no longer matters.
A flat edge list searched linearly for every query.

feedback.reason: High density, affordable O(V²) storage, and dominant constant-time edge-membership queries cross the boundary where a matrix is appropriate.

blocks.text: The dominant query changes the representation boundary

items: A matrix stores a boolean at [u][v], so one direct edge-membership query takes O(1).
For V = 2,000, the matrix has V² = 4,000,000 cells, which the prompt explicitly permits.
A near-complete directed graph already has Θ(V²) edges, so adjacency-list edge entries also occupy Θ(V²) total space.

blocks.text: The offered adjacency list is unsorted, so checking u → v can scan up to u's entire outgoing list, Θ(V) in this dense case. Repeating that work millions of times is exactly what direct matrix indexing avoids. Running BFS asks whether a path exists, not whether the single edge u → v exists, so traversal precomputation solves a different and more expensive problem.

blocks.title: Matrix boundary
blocks.text: A matrix is justified when quadratic storage is affordable and direct membership queries dominate; it is not categorically right or wrong.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.adjacency_list: Adjacency lists remain valid, but each membership query may scan a long neighbor list; the premise explicitly makes matrix storage affordable and membership dominant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.edge_list: A flat edge list makes each membership query proportional to E and ignores the repeated-query requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_precompute: Traversal choice does not remove the need to store or query edges, and all-sources traversal would be far more work than direct matrix lookup.

items.prompt: A 4,000 × 4,000 grid allows movement to an in-bounds, non-blocked orthogonal neighbor. The task will traverse reachable cells once. How should the graph normally be represented?

options.text: Store only a visited set; marking on dequeue is equivalent to representing the edges.
Materialize an adjacency matrix with one row and column for every grid cell.
Treat every row as a tree and use parent links between cells.
Treat each cell as a state and generate up to four legal neighbors when the cell is expanded.

feedback.reason: The grid supplies an implicit bounded-degree graph, so legal neighbors can be generated on demand without materializing edges.

blocks.text: The movement rule is already an edge generator

items: Treat an in-bounds, non-blocked cell (r, c) as a vertex.
For each of the four offsets (−1, 0), (1, 0), (0, −1), and (0, 1), compute a candidate neighbor.
Keep the candidate only if it is in bounds and non-blocked, then let the traversal process it subject to visited state.

blocks.text: The grid has 16 million possible cells, yet each expansion tests at most four moves in O(1). An adjacency matrix over those cells would have the square of 16 million entries, while a row-parent structure would lose vertical moves and cycles. A visited set records which states were discovered; it cannot replace the rule that defines legal edges.

blocks.title: Implicit-graph rule
blocks.text: Generate bounded local neighbors on demand unless transition computation is itself expensive enough to justify an index.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.full_matrix: The grid already defines local adjacency; a matrix over 16 million cells would be quadratic in the number of cells and unnecessary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.row_tree: Grid movement can create cycles and cross-row connections, so tree parent links do not encode the legal state graph.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.visited_as_representation: Visited state records discovery, not which moves are legal, and late marking can allow duplicate frontier entries.

items.prompt: Select all actions required to build an adjacency-list representation of an undirected graph with vertices 0 through n−1 from edge pairs {u, v}.
constraints: Every edge has distinct endpoints u and v in 0 through n−1, and no undirected edge is repeated.

options.text: Mark u and v visited while reading the edge so traversal cannot revisit them.
Create an empty neighbor collection for every vertex 0 through n−1.
For each {u, v}, add only v to u’s list because the input pair already names the edge.
For each {u, v}, add v to u’s list and u to v’s list.

feedback.reason: Undirected adjacency requires both directions, and the declared vertex set must exist even when a vertex has no incident edge.

blocks.text: Build the vertex set first, then add both incidences

items: Allocate n empty neighbor collections, one for every declared vertex 0 through n−1.
For each undirected edge {u, v}, append v to u's collection and u to v's collection.

blocks.text: Initialization preserves isolated vertices whose lists remain empty. Symmetric insertion makes the same undirected edge navigable from either endpoint; inserting only v under u instead represents a directed edge u → v. Visited state is mutable state for one traversal session and must not be set while the static graph is being built.

blocks.title: Separate two contracts
blocks.text: The representation stores every vertex and edge; a later traversal independently records which stored vertices it has discovered.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.append_input_direction_only: That construction represents a directed edge u → v and loses traversal in the reverse direction.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mark_visited_while_building: Visited state belongs to a particular traversal, not to the static representation; marking endpoints during construction would suppress valid exploration.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.initialize_all_vertices: Without entries for all n vertices, isolated vertices disappear from the representation.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.append_both_directions: An undirected edge must be available from either endpoint during neighbor iteration.

items.prompt: The input declares n = 6 vertices and gives only the undirected edges {0,1} and {1,2}. Which representation detail is necessary before counting connected components?

options.text: Create entries only for 0, 1, and 2 because only endpoints belong to the graph.
Represent all six vertices, including empty neighbor lists for 3, 4, and 5.
Store only 0 ← 1 ← 2 as a tree and infer the remaining vertices later.
Omit empty entries; BFS will discover the missing vertices faster than DFS.

feedback.reason: The vertex set is defined by n, not by the edge endpoints; isolated vertices are material graph states.

blocks.text: Edge endpoints do not define the whole declared vertex set

items: The edges connect 0, 1, and 2 into one component: {0, 1, 2}.
Vertices 3, 4, and 5 each have degree zero, so each empty neighbor list is a separate one-vertex component.
The correct whole-graph count is therefore four components.

blocks.text: Creating entries only for edge endpoints silently changes a six-vertex graph into a three-vertex graph. Neither BFS nor DFS can discover a state omitted from the representation, and a parent chain for the connected fragment cannot encode the three declared isolated vertices.

blocks.title: Whole-graph rule
blocks.text: When vertices are declared separately from edges, initialize from the vertex declaration and use edges only to add adjacency.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.endpoint_vertices_only: The declared vertex set includes 3, 4, and 5; each isolated vertex is a component and must remain visible.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_discovers_missing: No traversal can discover a vertex that was removed from the represented vertex set, and BFS versus DFS does not repair the omission.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.parent_chain: A tree fragment does not encode the declared isolated vertices or the full graph contract.

items.prompt: Which representation rule remains correct across sparse and dense graph tasks?

options.text: Choose the representation that makes BFS possible, because BFS is always faster than DFS.
Always choose adjacency lists because adjacency matrices are always wrong.
Choose from graph density, memory limits, and the dominant operations such as neighbor iteration or edge membership.
Representation is irrelevant if vertices are marked visited when dequeued.

feedback.reason: Representation is a cost-model decision driven by density, memory, and required operations, not by a universal graph slogan.

blocks.text: Match storage to the operation profile

items: Adjacency lists use O(V + E) space and expose actual neighbors efficiently, especially in sparse graphs.
Adjacency matrices use O(V²) space but answer direct edge membership in O(1), which can fit dense repeated-query workloads.
Implicit graphs compute legal transitions from a state and avoid storing edges that a simple rule can regenerate.

blocks.text: Choose by listing the dominant operations, estimating density and representation size, and then checking the memory limit. BFS versus DFS chooses expansion order after the graph interface exists; visited timing controls duplicate discovery. Neither decision erases storage or neighbor-access costs.

blocks.title: Reusable decision sequence
blocks.text: Name the operations first, quantify density and memory second, then select the representation that supports those operations within the constraints.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.lists_always: Lists are often appropriate, but dense graphs with affordable memory and dominant membership queries can justify a matrix.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_decides: Both traversals can use lists or matrices, and their full-traversal asymptotics are usually governed by representation rather than a universal speed ranking.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.visited_decides: Visited timing affects duplicate frontier work; it does not remove storage and neighbor-access costs.

items.prompt: A state is a four-wheel lock code. One move increments or decrements exactly one wheel, except that forbidden codes cannot be entered. The task asks whether a target code is reachable. What representation avoids unnecessary preprocessing?
constraints: Each wheel stores a decimal digit and changes modulo 10, so 0 decrements to 9 and 9 increments to 0.
Forbidden codes are excluded from generated neighbors.

options.text: Assign each code one parent because search states form a tree.
Use a queue as the representation; a queue makes the search BFS and therefore faster than DFS.
Prebuild an adjacency matrix over every pair of possible codes.
Represent a code as the state and generate its legal one-move neighbors when expanded.

feedback.reason: The transition rule computes a small neighbor set directly, so the state graph should remain implicit.

blocks.text: Generate the eight local transitions when needed

items: Use the four-digit code itself as the vertex state.
For each of four wheel positions, construct the result of adding 1 and subtracting 1 modulo 10.
Discard forbidden codes and expose the remaining candidates as this state's legal neighbors.
Let the traversal's visited set suppress states already discovered.

blocks.text: For example, changing the first wheel of 0000 produces 1000 and 9000 before forbidden-state filtering. The same constant-size rule produces at most eight candidates for any code, so prebuilding pairwise adjacency over all 10,000 codes adds work without improving neighbor access. A parent pointer or queue records search history or order; neither defines all legal transitions.

blocks.title: State-space rule
blocks.text: When a compact deterministic rule generates neighbors, keep the graph implicit and keep transition, visited, and frontier responsibilities separate.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_codes_matrix: Most code pairs are not adjacent; local transition generation is direct and avoids quadratic preprocessing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.single_parent: A code can be reached by many move sequences and cycles are possible, so one static parent does not represent all transitions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.queue_is_graph: A queue controls traversal order but does not define which code transitions are legal.
